paper_summary: This paper presents GRADINO, a from-scratch generator and benchmark framework for controlled numerical question answering over multiple non-relational tables. GRADINO synthesizes a latent relational source to compute executable SQL supervision and gold answers, then renders multiple perturbed non-relational views (pivots, hierarchical headers, merged cells, typographical noise, blank rows/columns, unit conversions, OCR-like errors). It generates parallel (one scalar per table aggregated by sum/avg/max/min) and sequential (lookup chains across tables) multi-table instances, verbalizes questions via an LLM and verifies them, and evaluates LLMs only on the perturbed non-relational views. The authors evaluate gpt-5-mini and several Qwen models on environmental and financial domains across varied table counts and perturbations, showing sharp accuracy drops with increasing table count and with unit heterogeneity, and that sequential chains are harder than parallel aggregation. They validate generation quality via manual inspection (~95.9% correct), show GRADINO data can improve finetuned models on a real benchmark, and provide detailed prompts and appendices.
summary_of_strengths: 1) Novel generation design: decouples verifiable SQL supervision from non-relational presentation by synthesizing a latent relational source and rendering perturbed views, enabling controlled multi-table diagnostics. 2) Important empirical finding: demonstrates a substantial and compounded failure mode for LLMs on multi-table non-relational numerical reasoning (scaling collapse and large unit-heterogeneity effects), with cross-model experiments and real-table validation. 3) Utility: generator can produce configurable datasets useful for evaluation and finetuning; experiments show GRADINO complements scarce real data. 4) Thoroughness: multiple ablations (table count, parallel vs sequential, units), manual verification, full prompt and appendix details, and discussion of limitations and ethics.
summary_of_weaknesses: 1) Synthetic realism: GRADINO is intentionally synthetic and diagnostic; the generated tables may not capture all distributional, visual, and semantic complexities of real-world reports or spreadsheets, limiting external validity for some deployments. 2) Domain breadth: experiments are limited to two domains (environmental, finance); generalization to other domains or settings (e.g., healthcare) is not shown. 3) Simplified sequential topology: sequential instances enforce unique lookup matches to control difficulty; this reduces realism relative to many real-world multi-join scenarios. 4) Generator & verifier dependence on LLMs: schema, constraints, and question verification rely on an LLM (gpt-5-mini), which can introduce biases and potential model-favoring artifacts; the authors discuss and partially mitigate this but residual bias is possible. 5) Missing certain presentation cues: the rendering does not model all visual/layout cues (alignment, charts mixed with tables) which can be important in practice. 6) Reproducibility sensitivity: while prompts and many details are provided, full replication depends on the authors’ planned release of code/data and exact solver/seed settings.
comments_suggestions_typos: Overall well written with extensive appendices and reproducibility-oriented materials. Suggestions: 1) Emphasize early in the introduction that GRADINO is primarily a diagnostic/synthetic generator (not a replacement for curated real datasets). 2) In figures, ensure clear legend/line markers for grayscale viewing. 3) Include (in the public release) runnable scripts for the constraint-solver sampling and generation filtering thresholds to aid reproduction. No major typos noted.
limitations_and_societal_impact: The authors explicitly discuss limitations: synthetic realism, restricted numerical focus, question-verbalization errors, generation/discard costs, and perturbation coverage. They also discuss ethical considerations clearly: generated data is synthetic (no PII), real tables used for validation come from public sources, and use is research-only. One missing nuance: potential bias introduced by synthetic unit distributions and the risk that finetuning on synthetic perturbations could overfit to those patterns rather than natural noise; the authors partially mitigate this by combining GRADINO and real data in experiments.
ethical_concerns: No major ethical concerns. The dataset is synthetic, contains no PII, and the authors respect dataset licenses and discuss risks (e.g., misinterpretation of synthetic benchmark results).
